strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple benchmarks, architectures, and scales, with impressive efficiency gains (1.26B matching 2.8B performance with 55% fewer parameters)
Well-executed technical approach using Jacobi iteration for parallelization, with clear mathematical justification and demonstrated rapid convergence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including large-scale pretraining, extensive downstream tasks, instruction-following benchmarks, and thorough ablation studies
Excellent reproducibility with provided code, detailed hyperparameters, and clear methodology presentation
Validated generalization across Pythia, LLaMA, and GPT-2 architectures, plus successful application to continual pretraining of existing models
weaknesses: Insufficient theoretical justification for why feeding hidden states as embeddings improves performance; lacks mechanistic explanation and analysis of what latent thoughts actually learn

Training-inference mismatch: Jacobi iteration approximates fixed-point hidden states during training but inference uses sequential single-pass generation; approximation quality not verified for downstream tasks
Limited evidence of scalability beyond 1.4B parameters; primary experiments and appendix scale only to 1.4B, with continual pretraining using only 5B tokens on a 3B model

Practical efficiency claims need clarification: Table 3 shows lower throughput (111.55 vs 110.50 tokens/s) than LLaMA-2.8B despite efficiency gains; sequential inference latency not fully captured in FLOP analysis

Moderate novelty: core concept of recurrent hidden-state computation builds incrementally on existing work (Universal Transformers, PonderLM); Jacobi iteration is a known technique applied to this setting
Critical design choice (position embedding reuse) justified only by 'negligible difference' on small models (Pythia-70M with 30B tokens); implications for long-context capabilities unexplored
Missing interpretability analysis: no visualization or probing of latent thought representations; no investigation of which positions benefit most or when latent computation helps/hurts
Baseline comparisons use reported numbers for some methods (PonderLM) rather than reimplementation; some baselines (OPT, Bloom) trained on different data amounts

strengths: Novel per-token latent thought approach well-motivated by CoT success
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (Pythia, LLaMA, GPT-2) and diverse downstream tasks
Strong empirical scaling results: 1.4B model matches 2.8B baseline with 55% fewer parameters on language modeling
Reproducibility: source code provided with specified hyperparameters
Practical validation beyond controlled settings: continual pretraining on LLaMA-3-3B demonstrates applicability
Systematic ablation studies analyzing Jacobi iterations and latent thought chains
Generalization demonstrated across different model sizes and training datasets
weaknesses: Fundamental training-inference mismatch: Jacobi iteration finds fixed-point hidden states during training, but inference uses sequential generation without iteration. The paper does not adequately justify why this inconsistency should be benign or provide theoretical analysis of gradient flow implications

Inference efficiency claims are misleading: Table 3 shows 2× throughput degradation (221→111 tokens/s), meaning actual wall-clock inference time doubles. Emphasis on 'identical inference cost' refers only to FLOPs, not practical deployment efficiency

No analysis of what latent thoughts represent: missing visualization, semantic interpretation, or investigation of whether improvements come from meaningful intermediate reasoning or simply from additional computation per token

Limited algorithmic novelty: core idea (use h_i to predict x_{i+1}) is straightforward; main contribution is applying standard Jacobi iteration to parallelization. Primarily an engineering contribution
Statistical significance not established: all results from single runs with no error bars; many downstream improvements are modest (1-4%) and could be within noise
Ad-hoc design choices: position embedding strategy (reusing token position for latent thoughts) lacks theoretical justification; K ∈ {2,3,4} sampling unexplained with no sensitivity analysis
Missing analysis of training efficiency: no discussion of training time, GPU memory requirements, or whether computational savings from parallelization are offset by iterative overhead

Incomplete comparison with related work: distinction from Coconut claimed but not experimentally validated; missing direct evaluation on reasoning-focused tasks where latent thinking should provide clearest benefits

strengths: Novel conceptual framework distinguishing 'horizontal' (per-token computation in continuous space) from 'vertical' (layer reuse) scaling with clear motivation and intuitive approach

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple architectures (Pythia, LLaMA, GPT-2), large-scale pretraining (300B tokens), extensive downstream benchmarks (9 tasks), instruction-following evaluation, and proper baseline comparisons

Strong empirical results showing 1.4B model matches 2.8B baseline with 55% fewer parameters, consistent improvements across model sizes, and superiority over stronger baselines with higher inference costs
Clever use of Jacobi iteration for efficient parallel training, with demonstrated rapid convergence and practical scalability
Well-written paper with clear motivation, effective visualizations, comprehensive related work taxonomy, provided code, and detailed hyperparameters enabling reproducibility
Validation on off-the-shelf models (LLaMA-3-3B) and demonstration of applicability via continual pretraining increases practical impact
weaknesses: 'Identical inference cost' claim is misleading—the method requires two forward passes per token (one for latent thought generation, one for next token), and Table 3 shows actual throughput is lower than baselines (111.55 vs 221.19 tokens/s), contradicting the central cost efficiency claim

Insufficient analysis of the train-test mismatch: training uses parallel Jacobi iteration (K∈{2,3,4}) while inference is purely sequential; the approximation error, convergence guarantees, and sensitivity to K distribution are unexplored

Limited theoretical justification for why feeding hidden states back as embeddings works—no mechanistic explanation, comparison to deeper models with equivalent FLOPs, or analysis of what latent thoughts learn and represent

Position embedding strategy is underexplored: reusing token position IDs for latent thoughts seems semantically problematic, ablation provides no quantitative comparison, and scalability to longer sequences is uncertain

Experimental design concerns: PonderLM comparisons use published results rather than controlled re-implementation; LLaMA baselines train on 26B tokens vs 300B for others (incomparable settings); some baseline implementations appear custom rather than official

Scalability and generalizability unclear: all experiments limited to ≤1.4B parameters; performance at 7B+ scale unknown; position embedding limitations may become critical for longer sequences; no wall-clock training time comparisons provided
